newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says talks only likely after China meeting.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says talks only likely after China meeting.

text.p: Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui said on Thursday that Taipei and Beijing were unlikely to resume serious dialogue until after China's communist leaders settled their differences during a key party congress this October.

Lee told a group of Japanese journalists that the resumption of "constructive negotiations" across the Taiwan Strait would likely take place after the 15th Communist Party Congress, a statement issued by the Presidential Office said.
The party congress was slated for October.

China's belated responses to Taiwan's proposals, including Lee's offer to embark on a "journey of peace" to the mainland, showed no consensus among the communist leaders, the statement quoted Lee as saying.
A furious China froze semi-official talks with Taipei after Lee made a landmark private visit to the United States in mid-1995.

Communist China, which has viewed Nationalist Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949, saw Lee's trip as promoting independence for the island rather than reunification with the mainland.

Beijing held war games and live-fire missile tests in waters near Taiwan between August 1995 until the run-up to the island's March 1996 presidential election -- the first time a Chinese government had seated its leader through popular suffrage.
Beijing acknowledged the eight months of manoeuvres were a bid to intimidate Taiwan voters against seeking independence.
Taiwan has repeatedly urged China to resume talks to resolve thorny issues facing both sides, including fishing disputes, repatriation of hijackers and stowaways.

But Beijing has consistently declined, saying no talks were possible until Taiwan showed its sincerity by halting its drive to enter the United Nations, its courtship of ties with other countries and other "splittist" activities.
During the interview with Japanese media, Lee reiterated the government's caution over Taiwan's investment in the mainland.
"Any investment in the mainalnd must be careful," Lee was quoted as saying.

"Those who view the mainland's 1.2 billion population as a huge market and recklessly invest there without evaluating its purchase power, social and political factors will pay a heavy price," Lee said.

Some 30,000 Taiwan firms have poured more than US$30 billion in mainland investments since a political thaw begun in the late 1980s. Taiwan worries that over-dependence on the mainland will make the island politically vulnerable.

Mainland China on Thursday gave six Taiwan shipping firms approval to sail direct Taiwan-China routes for the first time in 48 years, reciprocating for similar permits issued by Taipei to five mainland carriers.
Executives said sailings could begin in the next few days.
